procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated January 18, 1968 of the Allahabad High Court in Criminal Revision No. 1482 of 1966, acquitting the respondent of an offence punishable under s. 14 of the Foreigners Act (Act No. 31 of 1946).
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The City Magistrate convicted the respondent under s. 14 of the Foreigners Act. The Sessions Judge upheld the conviction. The High Court, in revision, disagreed with the lower courts and set aside the conviction.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The State of U.P. appealed to the Supreme Court on a certificate of fitness granted by the Allahabad High Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether a person, who was a citizen of India at the commencement of the Constitution, could be treated as a foreigner and prosecuted under the Foreigners Act before the Central Government determined that they had acquired the citizenship of a foreign country.

facts: The respondent was a citizen of India when the Constitution commenced in 1950.
He entered India in 1955 on a Pakistani passport and overstayed the permitted period.
In 1963, criminal proceedings were initiated against him under the Foreigners Act.
While these proceedings were pending, the Central Government determined in November 1964 that the respondent had acquired Pakistani citizenship before March 1955.
law: The Supreme Court relied on its previous rulings which established that the question of whether an Indian citizen has lost their citizenship by acquiring that of a foreign country must be determined exclusively by the Central Government under Section 9 of the Citizenship Act, 1955.
Until the Central Government makes this determination, the person cannot be treated as a foreigner.
application: The Court applied this legal principle to the timeline of the case. When the respondent was prosecuted in 1963 for overstaying, the Central Government had not yet determined his citizenship status.
Therefore, at the time the prosecution began, he could not legally be treated as a foreigner.
The subsequent determination by the Central Government in 1964, while final, could not have a retrospective effect to make an act a penal offense when it was not one at the time of its commission.
In essence, the respondent could not be prosecuted for being a foreigner until he was officially declared to be one by the proper authority.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that a person who was an Indian citizen at the commencement of the Constitution could not be treated as a foreigner and prosecuted under the Foreigners Act until the Central Government had first determined that they had lost their Indian citizenship by acquiring a foreign one. Since the prosecution in this case was initiated before the Central Government's determination, the conviction was invalid.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a person, who was a citizen of India at the commencement of the Constitution, could be treated as a foreigner and prosecuted under the Foreigners Act before the Central Government determined that they had acquired the citizenship of a foreign country.
appellant_arguments: The determination made by the Central Government under s. 9(2) of the Citizenship Act is final.

Since the Central Government determined that the respondent had acquired citizenship of Pakistan before March 15, 1955, his entry into India and subsequent overstay after that date constituted an offense punishable under s. 14 of the Foreigners Act.
respondent_arguments: The respondent was an Indian citizen at the commencement of the Constitution and was not a foreigner when he entered India in 1955.
The respondent could only be considered to have lost his Indian citizenship after the Central Government's determination on November 5, 1964.
Therefore, he could not be prosecuted under the Foreigners Act for acts (entry and overstay) committed in 1955, a time when he had not yet been determined to be a foreigner.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The question as to whether a person has lost citizenship of this country and has acquired the citizenship of a foreign country must be decided by the Central Government. It is only after the Central Government has decided this point that any other authority can take action against the person as a foreigner.
obiter: In dealing with the question of citizenship, the Central Government would be entitled to give effect to the impugned R. 3 in Sch. III and deal with the matter in accordance with the other relevant Rules framed under the Act.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The determination by the Central Government that a person has acquired foreign citizenship does not have a retrospective effect. It cannot retroactively render an act, which was not a penal offense at the time of its commission, into a criminal offense. Therefore, a person who was an Indian citizen at the commencement of the Constitution cannot be prosecuted under the Foreigners Act for acts like overstaying a visa committed before the Central Government officially determined that they had lost their Indian citizenship.
legal_tests_applied: The decision of the Central Government about the status of the person is the basis on which any further action can be taken against him.
A determination of foreign citizenship by the Central Government cannot have the effect of retrospectively rendering a penal offence an act which was not so at the time of its commission.
why_appellant_lost: The prosecution was for overstaying in 1955, but at that time, the respondent had not been determined to be a foreigner by the Central Government.
The Central Government's determination in 1964 that the respondent had acquired foreign citizenship could not retroactively criminalize the respondent's act of overstaying in 1955.
No directions under the law governing foreigners were given to the respondent after the determination on November 5, 1964, which he could have disobeyed to entail a new prosecution.
why_respondent_won: Till the Central Government determined the question of his lost Indian nationality, he could not be treated as a foreigner and no penal action could be taken against him on the basis of his status as a foreigner.

The respondent was an Indian citizen when he entered India in 1955 and could not be convicted of overstaying in this country at least till he was duly found to be a Pakistani national and to have ceased to be an Indian citizen.
The wide charge as framed against him was misconceived because the act of overstaying was not a penal offense for him at the time it was committed.
policy_considerations: The respondent even though held to be a Pa-kistani, and therefore a foreigner, before the charge was framed against him is entitled to the protection of our laws.
